headline: Stonington breakwater at first light: bass hunker in the shadows, bonito knocking from the east
subhead: Warm water has the boulder fields playing a waiting game, but the tide swings building toward full moon are about to change the math.
body_markdown:
The bait tells you everything before you ever see a fish. Right now around the boulder fields of Fishers Island Sound, the peanut bunker and silversides are still loose and scattered — not tight, not nervous, not pushed into the corners the way they get when albies or bonito show up and start working them. That's the read for this week: close, but not here yet. New London is holding at 69.4 degrees, which is cool enough on the eastern end of the Sound to keep things interesting but not cool enough yet to trigger the real turn. Kings Point to the west is running 70.9, and that gradient matters — it's the kind of west-to-east temperature drop that eventually funnels bait and predators toward the Race, and Fishers Island Sound sits right in that pipeline.

Striped bass are in their predictable late-August posture — daytime fish tucked deep against rock, feeding hard only in short windows around the tide change, and the better grade of fish sliding into a night program. This isn't the fall push. It's the holding pattern before it. We said as much a few days back — this stretch of summer has bass sitting tight rather than migrating, and that's exactly what the boulder fields are showing. Anyone fishing the granite structure off Ram Island or the rockpiles tight to Wamphassuc Point during daylight is finding fish, but they're finding them shallow-holding in the shade lines and current breaks, not roaming and feeding on top. Eels drifted slow along the drop-offs on the last two hours of the ebb have been the most consistent producer after dark, fished on light spinning gear so the eel can work naturally through the rocks instead of getting horsed over them. During the day, a bucktail in the 3/4- to 1-ounce range, white or olive, cast tight to the rock edges on the Stonington Breakwater and allowed to tick bottom on the retrieve has been picking off fish in the mid-20s to low-30s, mostly on the last of the outgoing when current pulls bait off the stone.

The breakwater itself has been the most dependable piece of structure in the zone all week — both the east and west walls are holding fish on the slack and the beginning of the new tide, when the current isn't ripping too hard to hold a jig down in the rock seams. Once the tide really starts moving, especially with the moon building toward full and the swings getting more aggressive over the next few days, that bite tightens into shorter windows but gets more concentrated. That's worth planning around — if you've only got one tide this weekend, fish the hour before and after the change rather than the peak of the flow.

Fluke are the disappointment of the month, and it's not just a Stonington problem — this warm-water stretch has spread fluke out across flats and open bottom from here down through Long Island rather than letting them stack. Little Narragansett Bay and the deeper cuts near the Mystic River channel are still worth a drift with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, but the fish are thin and scattered compared to a normal late August. The better fluke have been coming from the deeper humps inside Fishers Island Sound proper, where a cooler bottom layer persists even with the surface running warm — that's the pattern to lean on until temperatures break.

Blackfish are around the same rock piles they always are, but with water this warm they're not the target right now — they'll matter again once the fall bite firms up and the cooler water pulls them back onto the structure in earnest. Sea bass are a steady secondary catch on the deeper rock and reef structure scattered through the Sound, and that's held true all week — nothing spectacular, but a reliable fill-in while you wait on bigger things.

And the bigger thing everyone in Stonington is actually watching for is bonito and false albacore. Nothing's confirmed inside the Sound yet, but the early word out of Block Island and Point Judith has bonito showing, and that's precisely the signal we flagged — this stretch of warm water peaking and starting its seasonal slide was supposed to push that bite west into eastern Long Island Sound within a week or two, and the reports out of Rhode Island's south shore right now are the leading edge of exactly that. Fishers Island Sound sits close enough to the Race and its current to be next in line. Watch the bait around Esker Point and the open water off Watch Hill — when the silversides start balling up tight and nervous instead of scattered, that's the tell. Have a 2- to 3-inch epoxy jig or a Deceiver-style fly ready, because once albies show in this stretch they don't give you much warning and they don't stick around long once the tide turns against them.

Look for the next few days to hold mostly steady — light southwest wind, stable pressure, warm surface water — with the tide swings sharpening as the moon fills out. That's good news for the breakwater and rock-edge bass bite on the turns, and it's the kind of current strength that tends to pull bonito and albies in behind the bait once they're ready to move. If there's one window worth protecting this week, it's the last two hours of the evening ebb around the breakwater and Ram Island — that's where the structure, the tide, and the bait are lining up closest to right.
